title: The Physical AI Landscape & Embodiment
blurb: Tests how physical AI differs from digital AI, the sense-plan-act loop, degrees of freedom, open-loop against closed-loop control, PID and its three terms, why control runs at a fixed high rate, forward kinematics, and the sim-to-real gap.

questions.prompt: What does the chapter say makes physical AI different from digital AI?
options: A different kind of machine learning, with no gradient descent or attention involved
The system around the model: sensing, timing and physical stakes
Physical AI models are always much larger than those used in digital AI
Physical AI uses only classical algorithms, never learned models of any kind
questions.explanation: The models use the same primitives as Books 1–3. What changes is what they sense, how fast they must act, and what happens when they're wrong.

questions.prompt: What is physical AI's version of train/serve skew?
options: The gap between simulation and reality
Concept drift in user preferences
Prompt injection through sensors
Label lag in sensor data
questions.explanation: A simulator is a model of physics, never physics itself. A policy can learn to exploit simulator quirks that don't exist on real hardware.

questions.prompt: In the sense-plan-act loop, what does the "sense" stage do?
options: Trains the policy in simulation before deployment
Decides what the robot should do next, given what it knows
Turns raw sensor signal into a model of the world
Turns a decision into motor commands for the actuators
questions.explanation: Sense is perception (Chapter 59). Plan covers world models and VLAs. Act is where policies produce motor commands. Simulation is where the loop is practised, not a stage of it.

questions.prompt: How many degrees of freedom does an arm need to reach any position and any orientation in 3D space?
questions.explanation: 3 for position plus 3 for orientation. That is why 6-DOF arms are the industrial standard. 7+ DOF arms are redundant, with infinitely many joint solutions for one pose.

questions.prompt: What does adding degrees of freedom cost?
options: Less dexterity, since each joint limits the others more
A smaller workspace, since more joints means shorter links
Nothing, since control software scales freely with joints
A harder control problem, with more to get right
questions.explanation: More DOF brings dexterity and a larger workspace, but every DOF is another value a policy must set correctly, many times a second.

questions.prompt: What is the weakness of open-loop control?
options: It needs a sensor reading on every cycle.
It reacts too strongly to measurement noise.
Errors pile up, since nothing is checked.
It only works for systems with many DOF.
questions.explanation: Open-loop issues commands blindly. Uneven floors or weak motors cause drift with nothing to correct it, which is dead-reckoning.

questions.prompt: With real friction 4x what it assumed, open-loop reached 1.199 and closed-loop PID 5.003 (target 5.0). Why did PID cope?
options: It needs an accurate measurement of the error, not an accurate model.
Its gains were tuned for exactly that friction value beforehand.
It ran at a higher control frequency than the open-loop run did.
It knew the true friction from a separate sensor during the run.
questions.explanation: Closed-loop trades predicting the world correctly for measuring the error and correcting it. That is the chapter's central argument.

questions.prompt: Even with a matching friction model, open-loop only reached 4.171 of 5.0. Why?
options: The simulation had a bug that stopped it short of the target.
Open-loop controllers can never move a mass at all.
Friction varies with speed, so one fixed force can't fit.
The open-loop controller ran for fewer steps than the PID.
questions.explanation: A single precomputed force can't track a force that varies through the run. Closed-loop control adjusts every step.

questions.prompt: Which PID term can drive steady-state error to zero against a constant disturbance?
options: The derivative term
None of them; only a model can
The proportional term
The integral term
questions.explanation: The integral keeps accumulating while any error remains, so it grows until it cancels the disturbance. Proportional alone settles with an offset.

questions.prompt: A P-only controller with kp = 8 holds a mass against a constant bias force of −3. At equilibrium, kp × error must cancel the bias. What is the steady-state error?
questions.explanation: 8 × e = 3, so e = 0.375. The worked example's 0.3857 after 2,000 steps is approaching this. The offset is structural, not a tuning mistake.

questions.prompt: What does the derivative term do, and what is its risk?
options: Speeds up the response, but makes the system oscillate
Removes steady-state error, but causes integral windup
Damps oscillation and overshoot, but amplifies sensor noise
Predicts the target, but needs a model of the plant
questions.explanation: The derivative of a noisy measurement is more noise. Windup belongs to the integral term, and speed with oscillation to the proportional term.

It clamps the integral to a fixed limit.
It resets the integral to zero every second.
It lowers kp whenever the system overshoots.
questions.explanation: np.clip keeps the integral within ±integral_limit, so it can't grow without bound and cause slow, hard-to-damp oscillation.

questions.prompt: Why do control loops run at a fixed, high frequency? Select all that apply.
options: A late correction is a wrong correction, since the world doesn't pause
A fixed rate removes the need for any sensor at all
Stability analysis generally assumes a fixed, known period
Learned policies must fit their inference inside the loop's budget
questions.explanation: These are the chapter's three reasons. Closed-loop control needs measurements every cycle, which is the opposite of the fourth option.

questions.prompt: Which task typically needs the fastest control loop?
options: Planning a route across a map
Navigation and path following, 10–50 Hz
High-level task selection, 1–10 Hz
Balance and legged locomotion
questions.explanation: A balance controller has milliseconds before the robot falls. Task selection and route planning can be far slower.

questions.prompt: What is the main mitigation for the sim-to-real gap?
options: Domain randomisation of physics, lighting and textures
Running the real robot at a lower control rate
Training longer in a single, highly accurate simulator
Removing sensors so the policy can't overfit to them
questions.explanation: Varying the simulated world stops the policy overfitting to any one simulator's quirks. Chapter 62 covers it fully.

questions.prompt: In forward_kinematics, why does cumulative_angle accumulate instead of using each theta alone?
options: Each link's length depends on the angles before it.
Angles must be summed to convert them from degrees to radians.
It keeps the arm from crossing over itself.
Each angle is relative to the previous link.
questions.explanation: Procedure 58.3's common mistake is treating joint angles as global. Each link's direction is the sum of all joint angles up to it.

questions.prompt: A 2-link arm has l1 = 1.0 and l2 = 0.8, with θ1 = 90° and θ2 = 0°. What is the end effector's y position?
questions.explanation: Both links point straight up: y = 1.0 sin 90° + 0.8 sin(90° + 0°) = 1.0 + 0.8 = 1.8, with x = 0.

questions.prompt: How does inverse kinematics differ from forward kinematics?
options: It always has exactly one solution, found in closed form.
It needs no link lengths, only the target position.
It can have zero, one or two solutions.
It is the same calculation run on angles in degrees.
questions.explanation: Forward maps each joint configuration to one position. Inverse goes the other way, with elbow-up and elbow-down solutions for two links, and is numerical for longer arms.

bookExercises.prompt: Name the three stages of the sense-plan-act loop and, for each, name the chapter in this track that covers it.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Sense (turning raw sensor signal into a useful representation of the world) is covered by Chapter 59. Plan (deciding what to do next given that representation) is covered by Chapters 60-61. Act (turning a decision into motor commands) is covered by Chapter 63.

bookExercises.prompt: Explain in one or two sentences why a P-only controller cannot eliminate steady-state error against a constant disturbance, using the equilibrium argument from this chapter.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: At equilibrium, the proportional term `kp * error` must exactly balance the constant bias force for the system to hold still. If the error were zero, there would be no counter-force at all, and the bias force would immediately push the system away from zero again, so a nonzero error is required just to generate the counter-force needed to stay in place. This is structural, not a tuning failure; only the integral term, which keeps accumulating regardless of how small the current error is, can eventually cancel it.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 58.2, run the closed-loop simulation with `kp=8.0, ki=0.5, kd=4.0` (a smaller integral gain than the chapter's worked example) and describe, without running code if unavailable, whether you'd expect the final error to land between the full-PID value (-0.0016) and the P-only value (0.3857), and why.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A smaller `ki` (0.5 vs. 2.0) means the integral term accumulates counter-force more slowly, so the steady-state error would be expected to land somewhere between the full-PID result (-0.0016) and the P-only result (0.3857), closer to zero than P-only because there is still some integral action working to cancel the offset, but not as tight as `ki=2.0` because it takes longer for the accumulated integral to build up enough counter-force to fully cancel the bias.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 58.4 generalised to three links with `lengths=[1.0, 0.8, 0.5]` and `thetas` of 30°, -20°, and 45° (in that order, in radians), compute the end-effector position by hand or by tracing the accumulation logic.

A customer wants to skip simulation entirely and tune their robot's PID gains directly on hardware because "it's faster." Using this chapter's sim-to-real material, write the two or three sentences you'd say back, including one concrete risk.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Tuning directly on hardware skips the cheap, safe iteration simulation provides. Every bad gain choice during tuning is a real collision or a real fall, not a discarded simulation run. It also means starting from scratch with no prior estimate of reasonable gains, which is slower in practice than tuning roughly in simulation first and refining on hardware. Concrete risk: a `kp` set too high during live tuning can cause violent oscillation that damages the actuator or the arm itself before anyone can cut power.

bookExercises.prompt: A robot design review is deciding between a 6-DOF arm and a 7-DOF arm for a fixed pick-and-place task with no obstacles. Using the DOF trade-off discussion, argue for the 6-DOF choice.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: With no obstacles and a fixed task, the extra flexibility a 7th DOF provides, avoiding awkward configurations or obstacles for the same end-effector pose, has no work to do. The 6-DOF arm is exactly sufficient to reach any position and orientation the task requires, is cheaper to build, and has a control/planning problem with a unique (or at most doubly-valued) solution per target pose rather than the infinite family of solutions a redundant 7-DOF arm introduces, a strictly simpler problem for no lost capability given the constraints.

bookExercises.prompt: Read the relevant chapter of Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza on kinematics. Compare its treatment of inverse kinematics to this chapter's brief mention, and summarise in a few sentences why closed-form IK becomes impractical past 2-3 links.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only, no single answer. Closed-form inverse kinematics relies on being able to solve a system of trigonometric equations symbolically, which is tractable for 2 (and with effort, 3) links because the equations stay low-dimensional and the geometry is simple enough to enumerate the small number of solution branches (elbow-up/elbow-down) by hand. Past that, the equations become a coupled nonlinear system with no general closed-form solution, and the number of solution branches can grow or become degenerate (redundant arms have infinitely many). Numerical methods (e.g. Jacobian-based iterative solvers) trade an exact symbolic answer for an iteratively-refined numerical one that scales to arbitrary link counts.

bookExercises.prompt: A control loop is described as running at "10 Hz" for high-level planning and "500 Hz" for manipulator joint control. Explain why these two numbers are so different, using the control-loop-frequency table from this chapter.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: High-level planning (10 Hz) only needs to reconsider its decision a few times a second because the situation it's reasoning about, which task to do next, changes slowly. Manipulator joint control (500 Hz) is holding a physical system stable against continuous disturbances (gravity, contact forces, its own momentum) that must be corrected many times per second or the system diverges, the same open-loop-vs-closed-loop argument from this chapter, applied to loop rate rather than control strategy: a slow correction on a fast-changing physical quantity is effectively no correction at all.
